title: Why did Japan give up Taiwan... to no one?
fullText: in 1895 after losing a war to Japan rather badly China signed away the island of Taiwan in the treaty of Shimonoseki and at China's side of the table helping them work out the paperwork for handing over an island sat an American lawyer and former US Secretary of state fifty six years later when Japan signed the treaty that finally ended its ownership of Taiwan the man who wrote that treaty  was his grandson and that document gave the island up to legally speaking nobody at all so why  why did Japan give up Taiwan to no one so Japan ruled Taiwan as a colony for 50 years 50 years of railways sugar plantations and the sort of colonial rule that built infrastructure while shooting anyone who objected to it and during the Second World War the allies promised it back to China at the Cairo Conference in 1943 in a document that was technically a press release a detail governments would spend the next 80 years arguing about when Japan surrendered in 1945  China's Republic took over the island and annexed it almost immediately job done you'd think  except someone still had to write the actual peace treaty and before anyone got around to it China broke in half by 1949 the communists under Mao Zedong controlled the mainland while Chiang Kai shek's defeated nationalist government fled to of all places Taiwan both governments insisted that they and only they were China Britain recognized the one in Beijing America recognized the one in Taipei and then in June 1950 the Korean War broke out and President Truman sent the US Navy into the Taiwan Strait declaring that the island's future status must await the restoration of security in the Pacific a peace settlement with Japan or consideration by the United Nations which sounds very diplomatic and mostly meant we'll figure it out later the job of figuring it out later went to an American lawyer named John Foster Dulles who Truman put in charge of writing Japan's peace treaty and Dallas had a genuinely  unsolvable problem on his desk the treaty had to take Taiwan away from Japan that part everyone agreed on the question was what to write on the to whom line option 1 hand it to Chiang's Republic of China the government actually sitting on the island but Britain had already recognized Beijing and refused to sign anything implying Chiang was China Britain's Foreign Office had even told Parliament in public that Formosa was still legally speaking Japanese territory worse from Washington's view Chiang's government looked like it might collapse entirely  meaning Taiwan would be handed to a government that could stop existing  at which point the island and its rather useful position off the Chinese coast would fall to Mao and behind him the Soviets option 2  hand it to Mao's People's Republic America currently shooting at Chinese soldiers in Korea was not going to gift wrap an island for them option 3 write no treaty at all which would leave Japan under American occupation forever and Japan had some opinions about that the Americans had so little faith in Chiang that in early 1950 some in the State Department had quietly discussed backing a friendlier general to replace him The Korean War killed that idea in five weeks and since neither government could be invited to the peace conference without the other's supporters walking out the conference to decide China's former territory ended up including no China whatsoever which when writing a treaty about handing territory to China presented something of a spelling problem so Dallas every inch a lawyer reached for a lawyer's solution peace treaties normally use a very specific phrase territory is ceded to someone Shimonoseki the treaty his own grandfather had helped negotiate ceded Taiwan to Japan  name on the line clean transfer Donis deleted the recipient  the sentence he wrote Article 2 b of the treaty reads in full Japan renounces all right title and claim to Formosa and the Pescadores renounces not seeds not transfers not returns Japan simply lets go of the island and the island's ownership goes nowhere it hangs and this wasn't sloppy drafting look one line up but Article 2A Japan renounces Korea while recognizing Korean independence Korea's future got written into the sentence Taiwan's sentence just stops Dullis's actual plan sketched out in 1950 was that Taiwan's status would be settled afterwards by the United States Britain the Soviet Union and Chiang's Republic of China deciding together and if they couldn't agree within a year the question would be kicked up to the United Nations and here's the part that rarely gets mentioned Japan was quietly fine with this the Japanese government focused on trade rather than rearmament wanted to do business with both Chinese government and being legally required to pick a winner would have slammed one of those doors shut a vague renunciation meant Tokyo could give the island back without handing anyone a win so the one clause in the treaty that looks like a mistake was in fact the one clause that every single party in the room the Americans the British and the Japanese privately preferred the only people who might have objected were the two Chinas who conveniently weren't in the room on September 8th, 1951 48 nations signed the treaty of San Francisco the Soviet delegation attended objected at length that Taiwan should have been given to Beijing and then declined to sign Japan was free Taiwan was renounced and the to whom line stayed blank The US Senate however wanted one more thing dozens of senators warned they wouldn't ratify the treaty unless Japan made peace specifically with Chiang's government  so Japan did signing a separate treaty in Taipei  in April 1952 and notice what it did  even that treaty signed with the government actually running Taiwan just repeated that Japan had renounced the island it still didn't say Taiwan now belong to the Republic of China Japan had Learned the trick and it was sticking with it as for Dallas's tidy backup plan the four powers deciding together the one year clock the United Nations none of it ever happened the four powers never met on the question the clock ran out  nobody invoked the UN clause Taiwan simply stayed where the treaty left it renounced by Japan  governed by Chiang  claimed by Mao and legally speaking belonging to no one in 1955  Dulles by then US Secretary of state told a closed Senate hearing exactly what he'd done the treaty he said  ceded Taiwan to no one Japan merely renounced sovereignty over it and therefore he argued America could never accept that the fate of Taiwan was purely an internal matter for China the blank space wasn't a bug  it was the entire point a legal opening that kept the United States permanently entitled to an opinion and so 56 years after his grandfather sat in a treaty room watching Taiwan get handed to somebody John Foster Dulles sat in another one and made sure it was handed to nobody at all one family at both ends of the story the lawyer who signed Taiwan over to Japan and the grandson who signed it over to no one at all every legal argument about who owns Taiwan today starts from that missing name
